steps.body: You now own three tools for the same job. A **ratio table** shines when you want several rows at once. A **double number line** shines when the numbers live on a scale and you're reading between marks. Plain **find-the-multiplier** is fastest for a single question. Same relationship, same answers — pick whichever makes the arithmetic easiest.
Use a ratio table and scale both quantities together.

widget.prompt: The mix uses 2 cups of concentrate for every 5 cups of water. Complete the row for 8 cups of concentrate.
widget.successFeedback: 20 cups. Concentrate grew by ×4, and water grew by the same ×4, so the recipe relationship stayed unchanged.
widget.lowFeedback: Too little water. Follow the multiplier from 2 cups of concentrate to 8, then apply it to 5 cups of water.
widget.highFeedback: Too much water. Both columns must use the same scale factor.

hints: Find the multiplier from the concentrate.
explanationVariants: Whether by table row or multiplier, both parts take ×4.

predict.prompt: Scaling a recipe — must BOTH quantities scale by the same factor?

options.label: No — each scales its own way
No — add the same amount to both

predict.reveal: The relationship survives only if both quantities ride the same multiplier — quadruple the concentrate, quadruple the water. Different factors break the recipe.

explanationVariants: Five different party sizes means five rows — a table serves them all at once.
One row per party size beats five separate multiplier hunts.

widget.prompt: You need lemonade amounts for parties of 5 different sizes, all from one recipe ratio. Which tool fits the job best?

options.label: A ratio table — one row per party size
options.feedback: Right — tables hold many equivalent pairs at once; build five rows and read them off.

options.label: A double number line — read all five between the marks
options.feedback: The line CAN do it, but five reads between marks is slow work; a table lays all five rows out directly.

options.label: Adding the same amount for each bigger party
options.feedback: Adding breaks ratios entirely — bigger batches come from multiplying both quantities.

hints: How many answers do you need at once?
Five — which tool holds many pairs?

steps.body: Whatever the tool, the **check is the same**: shrink your answer pair to simplest form and it must match the original ratio. 8 : 20 shrinks (÷4) to 2 : 5 — the juice mix holds. An answer that won't shrink back was built by adding somewhere.

explanationVariants: 6 : 15 shrinks by ÷3 straight to 2 : 5 — it passes the shrink test.
Divide both by their common factor 3 and the original mix reappears.

widget.prompt: A classmate claims 6 cups concentrate with 15 cups water keeps the 2 : 5 mix. Does the shrink test agree?

options.label: Yes — 6 : 15 shrinks by ÷3 to exactly 2 : 5
options.feedback: Right — both parts divide by 3 and land on the original mix.

options.label: No — 6 : 15 shrinks to 3 : 5
options.feedback: 6 ÷ 3 = 2, not 3 — and 15 ÷ 3 = 5. The pair shrinks cleanly to 2 : 5, so it passes.

options.label: The test can't tell — the numbers are too big
options.feedback: The shrink test works at any size; that's the point. ÷3 lands 6 : 15 exactly on 2 : 5.

hints: Find a common factor of 6 and 15.

widget.prompt: Sort each situation to the tool that fits it most naturally.

items.label: One quick question: 3 : 7, first part is 21
items.feedback: A single question wants the fastest tool: 21 ÷ 3 = ×7, done. Tables and lines earn their setup only with more to read.

items.label: Batch sizes for 4 different bake sales
items.feedback: Many pairs at once is the table's home turf — one row per bake sale.

items.label: Reading a value BETWEEN two known marks on a scale
items.feedback: Between-the-marks is what a number line shows that a table hides — the in-between lives on the line.

items.label: Filling in a chart with 6 equivalent rows
items.feedback: Rows upon rows — the table again. Lines and lone multipliers would redo the work six times.

widget.missFeedback: Ask what the situation needs: one answer (multiplier), many rows (table), or an in-between reading on a scale (line).
widget.successFeedback: Sorted — same math, three shapes; fit the tool to the question.

explanationVariants: 21 ÷ 3 = 7, so the partner is 7 × 7 = 49 — one multiplication after one division.
The multiplier ×7 carries the 7 to 49 directly.

widget.prompt: Ratio 3 : 7. The first part is 21. What is the second part?

commonErrors.feedback: 25 keeps the 4-gap (21 + 4). The multiplier is 21 ÷ 3 = 7, so the partner is 7 × 7 = 49.
147 multiplies 21 × 7 — that's scaling the first part again. The 7 takes the ×7: 49.

explanationVariants: 9 : 12 shrinks to 3 : 4; of the candidates only 15 : 20 shrinks to 3 : 4 as well — 12 : 15 lands on 4 : 5 and 11 : 14 doesn't reduce there either.
Run every pair through the shrink test; one survivor.

widget.prompt: Which pair keeps the SAME relationship as 9 : 12?

options.feedback: Right — 15 : 20 shrinks (÷5) to 3 : 4, exactly where 9 : 12 (÷3) lands.
12 : 15 shrinks to 4 : 5 — it added 3 to each part of 9 : 12, the additive trap at chapter scale.
11 : 14 adds 2 to each part of 9 : 12 — and it can't shrink to 3 : 4 (11 and 14 share no factor with that target). The additive trap strikes again.

takeaways: Table for many rows; line for in-betweens; multiplier for one-shots.
Every tool multiplies both quantities — none of them add.
The shrink test verifies any answer: simplest form must match the original.
steps.teaser: next chapter: the same pairs again — this time as points on the coordinate plane.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Every tool asks the same question: what's the multiplier?** 2 : 5 with a first part of 6 means 2 × 3 = 6, so the partner is 5 × 3 = 15. Table, line, or head — the ×3 is the whole job.

commonErrors.feedback: 9 keeps the 3-gap (6 + 3). The multiplier is ×3 (2 × 3 = 6), so the partner is 5 × 3 = 15.
10 doubles the 5 — but 6 is 2 × THREE. The 5 takes the same ×3: 15.
